ann_85.original: Hypothesis: a linear layer of per-input terms; the analytical_formula evidence lists the terms. The largest is the international plan: its direct edge has weight 0.86 per sd and it has no other edge in the network, so for the typical customer having an international plan raises the predicted churn risk from 1.3% to 20.2%; removing that edge alone lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.861. Other usage terms per sd: total international charge 0.38, voice mail plan -0.31, total night charge 0.22, account length 0.14, total evening minutes 0.13, and total day minutes -0.40, which the day-evening hinge more than reverses for heavy users. State flags also have direct terms (for example -0.33 per sd for code 11 and -0.24 for Vermont, code 46); because a state flag is z-scored with a small share of customers, one sd is a small step and being in the state is a step of several sd, so these terms move the score a lot for the few customers in each state: moving the typical customer to Vermont lowers the predicted risk from 1.3% to 0.3% (whole model; Vermont also lowers the service-call chain through node 10379). Self-probe of additivity: the international plan shifts the score from -4.31 to -1.37 for a customer with 1 service call and from -1.91 to 1.03 with 5 calls, a parallel shift on the score scale. Switching the whole part off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.833.
ann_85.proposed: A sum of single inputs: an international plan raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves for a typical customer from about 1% to about 20%, and some states, a voice-mail plan and the usage totals move it by smaller amounts.

ann_86.original: Node 2016 ≈ relu(1.58 − 1.55·state:31) on the z-scored flag (the leaf's closed form is off by up to 0.0065, from rounding). Hypothesis: this part gives a few states their own churn offset, the largest for New Jersey (state code 31). Each hidden unit is a gate on one or a few state flags. Node 2016 is on for customers outside New Jersey and off inside it: 0 New Jersey customers have it on and 0 customers elsewhere have it off. It enters the score with a negative weight, so customers outside New Jersey carry a negative offset that New Jersey customers do not. Smaller gates add offsets for Washington (code 47, node 32834) and Iowa (code 12, node 827), and nodes 3620, 6606, 8711 and 9229 make small adjustments for West Virginia, Alaska and others. Two gates also feed other parts: node 20866 (Ohio, code 35) lowers the usage level, and node 10379 (Vermont, code 46) lowers the service-call chain at node 7689. Self-probe, moving the typical customer (a West Virginia customer, other inputs at typical values) between states: this part contributes -0.45 to the score in West Virginia, 2.49 in New Jersey, 1.14 in Washington and 0.44 in Iowa; the whole-model risk is 1.3%, 5.3%, 6.2% and 3.2%. New Jersey also has its own direct edge of -0.23 per sd (in direct_terms), which takes back part of this offset; the whole-model risks above include both. In the training data the 90 New Jersey customers have a churn rate of 24.4% against 13.9% elsewhere; Washington has 72 customers (churn rate 29.2%) and Iowa 55 (churn rate 10.9%), so each offset is fitted to the customers of one state; Iowa's positive offset is fitted to 55 customers whose churn rate is below the 14.2% of the rest of the data. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.910.
ann_86.proposed: This part gives a few states their own offset: for a typical customer, the predicted chance that a customer leaves goes from about 1% in West Virginia to about 20% in New Jersey, about 6% in Washington and about 3% in Iowa.

ann_87.original: Node 2899 ≈ relu(0.614·totalDayCharge − 0.963·numberVmailMessages − 0.0266·numberCustomerServiceCalls − 0.753), on z-scored inputs (off by up to 0.0005 on the training rows, from rounding the coefficients). Hypothesis: the model flags customers who spend a lot in the daytime and do not use voicemail; voicemail messages act as a veto. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): with no voicemail messages the part is off at a day charge of 30 US dollars (node value 0.00) and on at 35 US dollars (node value 0.10); at 55 US dollars the predicted churn risk is 72.3%, against 1.3% for the same customer with 30 voicemail messages, for whom node 2899 is still off (node value 0.00). In the training data the part acts on 1077 customers, whose churn rate is 26.9% against 9.4% for the other 2923; 1 of the customers it acts on has any voicemail messages. The service-call term has a very small weight and does not change this reading. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.892.
ann_87.proposed: Through this part, a higher daytime charge raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, with nothing until about 33.52 US dollars, then steadily. More voice-mail messages hold that rise back in an uneven way.

ann_88.original: Hypothesis: the model raises churn risk for customers who use the phone heavily in both the day and the evening. Node 1694 is a hinge on total day minutes plus evening charge; node 3237 is a second hinge on node 1694 that adds more for the heaviest users, so the part's push on the score grows faster than linearly once it is on. A higher evening charge lowers the day minutes needed to switch it on. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): at 180 day minutes and a 17-dollar evening charge node 1694 is off (value 0.00, risk 1.3%); at 270 day minutes the risk is 0.7% with a 12-dollar evening charge (node 1694 off, value 0.00), 3.6% with 17 dollars and 47.0% with 24 dollars; at 330 minutes and 24 dollars it is 95.8%. Day minutes also have their own direct edge of -0.40 per sd (in direct_terms), so below the hinge more day minutes slightly lower the score: with a 12-dollar evening charge the risk falls from 1.7% at 150 minutes to 0.7% at 270 minutes. Node 1694 also feeds the service-call alarm with a small positive weight. Three state flags (state codes 20, 27 and 35) shift the hinge threshold through node 28715 and a tiny edge; their effect on node 1694 is small. In the training data node 1694 is on for 805 customers, whose churn rate is 33.9% against 9.2% for the rest; node 3237 is on for 446, with churn rate 52.9%. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.890.
ann_88.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves for customers who use the phone heavily in both the day and the evening: more daytime minutes raise it, and even more so if the evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars, in a curve that is lowest at about 192 minutes and higher either side.

ann_89.original: Node 19579 ≈ relu(1.03·totalEveCharge + 1.02·relu(1.05·totalEveCharge − 0.386) − 1.05), on z-scored inputs (off by up to 0.042 on the training rows, from rounding), and it enters the score with a negative weight. Hypothesis: the model holds back the churn score of customers with a high evening charge, a counterweight to the evening charge's positive role in the day-evening hinge. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): the node is off at an evening charge of 20 US dollars (value 0.00, risk 1.3%) and on at 22 US dollars (value 0.95), where the predicted risk drops to 1.0% because the day-evening hinge is still off (node 1694 value 0.00); at 30 US dollars this part contributes -1.24 to the score, but node 1694 is on as well and the whole-model risk is 7.2%. In the training data the part acts on 956 customers, whose churn rate is 18.0% against 12.9% for the rest, so it pulls against the observed direction and acts as a partial offset rather than a churn signal of its own. Its effect is small: switching it off changes the training AUC from 0.9193 to 0.9192.
ann_89.proposed: A higher evening charge holds the predicted chance that a customer leaves back a little, with nothing until about 20.05 US dollars, then steadily.

ann_90.original: Hypothesis: node 4397 is a usage level that rises with the day charge and the evening charge, and its one outgoing edge goes into the service-call alarm (node 997) with a negative weight, so it suppresses that alarm for customers who use the phone a lot. The state flag for code 35 lowers the usage level through node 20866. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): with a 10-dollar evening charge the usage level is off at a day charge of 35 US dollars (value 0.00) and on at 40 US dollars (value 1.42); with a 25-dollar evening charge it is already on at a 20-dollar day charge (value 0.33) and reaches 7.50 at 45 US dollars. The typical customer's service calls are below the alarm's range, so the alarm is off and the usage level does not change that customer's prediction; it matters for customers with several calls (see service_calls_vs_usage). Switching the part off changes the prediction of 542 training customers, changes the mean predicted risk by -0.036 (with minus without) and lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.903.
ann_90.proposed: For the customers it acts on, a higher daytime charge lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves mostly in a jump around 27.49 US dollars (between 21.65 US dollars and 33.47 US dollars for different customers).

ann_91.original: Node 21178 ≈ relu(0.808·numberCustomerServiceCalls − 0.887) on the z-scored count (off by up to 0.0031 for the whole leaf, from rounding). Hypothesis: the model treats repeated customer-service calls as a churn alarm. Node 21178 is a step that switches on at the fourth call: it is on for the 318 training customers with 4 or more calls; 0 customers with 4 or more calls have it off, and 0 customers with fewer calls have it on. Node 997 is the stronger alarm: it grows with the number of calls (directly and through the chain 30505 to 7689) and is pushed down by the usage level (node 4397) and slightly up by the day-evening hinge (node 1694). Self-probe on the typical customer with a 15-dollar day charge (other inputs at typical values): the predicted risk is 1.3% at 2 calls, 5.0% at 3 calls, 52.8% at 4 calls and 96.0% at 5 calls; with a 35-dollar day charge node 997 is off at 4 calls (value 0.00) and the risk is 1.8%. In the training data the 318 customers with 4 or more calls have a churn rate of 50.0% against 11.1% for the rest. Node 997 also fires for 198 of the 530 customers with 3 calls; they have a churn rate of 6.6% but a mean predicted risk of 14.7%, so at 3 calls the alarm over-predicts. It fires for 0 customers with fewer than 3 calls. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.812; for comparison, switching off direct_terms lowers it to 0.833.
ann_91.proposed: Calls to customer service raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer this part acts on, from about 1% at 0 calls to about 6% at 3 calls, and to about 57% at four calls.

ann_92.original: Hypothesis: the service-call alarm and the usage level combine serially: the usage level feeds node 997 with a negative weight, so many service calls raise churn risk strongly for customers with low or average daytime spending and much less for heavy daytime spenders. Self-probe on the typical customer with 5 service calls (other inputs at typical values), sweeping the day charge: the predicted risk is 96.0% at 20 US dollars and 96.0% at 26 US dollars (usage level off, value 0.00), 29.8% at 30 US dollars and 2.0% at 32 US dollars, where node 997 has fallen to 0.02. The training data show the same split: of the customers with 4 or more calls, the 122 with the usage level off have a churn rate of 91.8% (mean predicted risk 82.5%), and the 196 with it on have a churn rate of 24.0% (mean predicted risk 25.0%). Switching the composition off lowers the training AUC from 0.919 to 0.812.
ann_92.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves for customers with several calls to customer service: for a typical customer it acts on (four calls), from about 1% without it to about 57% with it. A higher daytime charge takes most of that rise away, mostly in a jump around 27.49 US dollars (between 21.65 US dollars and 33.47 US dollars for different customers).

ann_93.original: Hypothesis: the churn score is the output bias plus the sum of the seven leaf parts' contributions, and the predicted risk is its sigmoid. Four signals carry most of the model: the international plan (a direct edge), many customer-service calls at low or average usage (service_calls_vs_usage), heavy daytime spending without voicemail (voicemail_day_charge), and heavy day-plus-evening use (day_eve_minutes_hinge); the state gates and the remaining direct terms adjust the score for smaller groups, and the evening-charge hinge is a small counterweight. Because the parts add on the score scale, two signals together raise the risk more than either alone on the probability scale. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): the predicted risk is 1.3% with no international plan and 1 service call, 20.2% with an international plan, 12.9% with 5 service calls and 73.6% with both. The full model has a training AUC of 0.919; switching off the parts one at a time gives the largest losses for service_call_alarm (AUC 0.812), direct_terms (0.833), day_eve_minutes_hinge (0.890) and voicemail_day_charge (0.892).
ann_93.proposed: The model adds up six parts: an international plan, several calls to customer service, heavy daytime spending without voicemail and heavy use in both the day and the evening raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves; state offsets adjust it, and a high evening charge holds it back a little. For a typical customer an international plan raises it from about 1% to about 20%.

parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the churn score is the output bias plus the sum of the seven leaf parts' contributions, and the predicted risk is its sigmoid. Four signals carry most of the model: the international plan (a direct edge), many customer-service calls at low or average usage (service_calls_vs_usage), heavy daytime spending without voicemail (voicemail_day_charge), and heavy day-plus-evening use (day_eve_minutes_hinge); the state gates and the remaining direct terms adjust the score for smaller groups, and the evening-charge hinge is a small counterweight. Because the parts add on the score scale, two signals together raise the risk more than either alone on the probability scale. Self-probe on the typical customer (other inputs at typical values): the predicted risk is 1.3% with no international plan and 1 service call, 20.2% with an international plan, 12.9% with 5 service calls and 73.6% with both. The full model has a training AUC of 0.919; switching off the parts one at a time gives the largest losses for service_call_alarm (AUC 0.812), direct_terms (0.833), day_eve_minutes_hinge (0.890) and voicemail_day_charge (0.892).
